analysis.one_liner: Requires cigarette makers to disclose additives and chemical contents on packages and in ads.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote; it sat in committee until the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required tobacco companies to list the chemical additives in their products and smoke on every package, and to disclose in advertising the health effects and warnings the government deems necessary. It would also have removed trade-secret protections from a report to Congress on tobacco additives. Manufacturers would have had 18 months' lead time before rules took effect. The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Health and the Environment Subcommittee, where it sat with no further action.
analysis.who_benefits: Smokers and nonsmokers exposed to secondhand smoke, who would learn exactly what chemicals are added to cigarettes and what is in the smoke — including substances like benzene, arsenic, and cyanide named in the bill's findings — instead of having that information kept as an industry trade secret.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Smokers and people exposed to secondhand smoke

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires manufacturers to identify chemical additives and constituents of tobacco products and smoke on each package, information that is currently not disclosed to the public.

It requires labeling, advertising, and promotion to carry adverse-effect information, warnings, directions for use, contraindications, and warnings against use with specific health conditions, as determined by the Secretary of Health and Human Services.

It strikes trade-secret and confidentiality protections from the existing report to Congress on tobacco additives, so that industry submissions about additives could be published rather than kept confidential.
Packages would have to carry a specific warning that, unlike food and other consumer products, cigarette additives have never been tested for their impact on human health when inhaled.

analysis.who_pays: Tobacco manufacturers, who would bear the cost of new labeling, advertising, and packaging and would lose the confidentiality of their additive submissions; some of that cost could be passed to consumers through prices.

drawbacks.text: Mandated warning and disclosure requirements impose compliance and printing costs on manufacturers, which companies can pass along to consumers through higher cigarette prices.

The bill delegates open-ended rulemaking to the Secretary of Health and Human Services — including 'any other information deemed necessary' — giving one executive official broad authority over tobacco labeling and advertising content.
Requiring disclosure of exact additive formulas raises trade-secret concerns for manufacturers competing over product recipes, an objection the industry raised against similar measures.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers, the benefit is plain information: what is actually in the cigarettes they or the people around them breathe. The costs — compliance expenses for manufacturers and possible price increases — are modest next to the information gain, and the strongest objection is the breadth of discretion handed to the Secretary rather than the disclosure itself. The disclosure provisions are the kind of regulation that is hard to argue against on the merits, which makes the bill's quiet death in committee more notable.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its health subcommittee in June 1994, and neither the subcommittee nor the full committee ever acted on it before Congress ended in January 1995.

narrative.text: Rep. Karen Shepherd introduced the Truth in Tobacco Labeling Act on June 27, 1994, joined by Representatives Waxman, Durbin, Synar, Meehan, Barrett of Wisconsin, and Hilliard as original cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day it was introduced.
On July 26, 1994, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health and the Environment, its last recorded action.
The bill received no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, and never reached the Senate; the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995, ending the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco manufacturers came out ahead: they kept chemical additive lists confidential as trade secrets, faced no new warning or disclosure requirements on packages or advertising, and the report on tobacco additives stayed confidential.

for.name: Rep. Karen Shepherd
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and originally cosponsored it with six colleagues.

for.name: 14 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Reps. Waxman, Durbin, Synar, Meehan, Barrett of Wisconsin, and Hilliard, who were original cosponsors.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Chaired by Rep. John Dingell; committee of referral
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to a markup or vote; it was passed down to a subcommittee, which also took no action.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat — the sponsor plus 14 Democratic cosponsors, no Republicans — but no committee or floor votes ever occurred, so the partisan shape of the opposition was never tested.

industries.note: The bill would have forced cigarette, cigar, and smokeless tobacco makers to print additive and smoke-constituent lists on packages, carry health warnings in advertising, and open their additive submissions to publication. Their interest in the bill ran against the public's, since their existing rights to keep additives as trade secrets is exactly what the bill existed to end.
The bill applies its disclosure requirements not just to labels but to advertising and promotion, requiring warnings and health information in marketing materials.
